blocks.text: Nor is there anyone who would willingly approach the hole of an asp or a basilisk. Or, if anyone were so mad, he would run a great risk to his life. Hence, to teach that there will be a great reversal of things under the kingdom of Christ, Isaiah says: Then the infant shall play על חור פתן, over the hole of the asp, and the child weaned from milk [col. 382] shall put his hand on the den of the basilisk, Es. XI, 8. That is, the Gentiles will come together with the Jews into one church [III, 158], and safe access will lie open to those who were once as terrifying to the faithful as the most venomous and deadly of snakes, namely asps and basilisks, are to children. Yet Sulpicius, in the first Dialogue, ch. 5, relates in these words that this was at some time also fulfilled literally: The abbot had sent bread by two boys, of whom the elder was fifteen years old and the younger twelve. As they were returning from there, an asp of wondrous size met them; they were not at all terrified at its approach, and when it came before their feet, as if charmed by incantations, it laid down its dark-blue neck. The younger of the boys seized it with his hand, wrapped it in his cloak, and began to carry it. Then, entering the monastery like a victor, he went to meet the brothers and, while all looked on, he unfolded his cloak and set down the captive beast, not without a swell of boasting. But Phylarchus, in Aelian, book 17, ch. 5, also relates that long ago in Egypt tame asps lived harmlessly with children, and when called by a snapping of the fingers crept out of their holes. His words are: Τοῖς παιδίοις (τὰς ἀσπίδας) συντρεφομένας μηδὲν ἀδικεῖν, καὶ καλουμένας δὲ ἐξέρπειν τῶν φωλῶν, καὶ ἀφικνεῖσθαι· κλῆσις δὲ αὐτῶν ὁ τῶν δακτύλων ἐστὶ κρότος [Tois paidiois (tas aspidas) syntrephomenas mēden adikein, kai kaloumenas de exerpein tōn phōlōn, kai aphikneisthai; klēsis de autōn ho tōn daktylōn esti krotos]. Lucan, book 9, line 909, reports the same of the Psylli:
— — — — the Psyllian holds these as pledges of his race: if any infant did not shudder at the snakes he touched, if any infant played with the serpents given to him.

And Aelian, History, book 1, ch. 57, says that the same people recognized their legitimate children by throwing them into a jar full of cerastes, from the fact that at their touch the cerastes ἐμαράνθησαν [emaranthēsan], wasted away. Indeed, even today in Africa, around Segelmessa, there are said to be fifteen mountains whose inhabitants live on familiar terms with serpents, so that children play with them. So relates Vincent le Blanc, part 2, ch. 23.
